about: The words the classes use, defined from the teachings and the King James text with the Apocrypha. Where the teaching goes beyond what the text itself says, the entry says so. Each entry links to moments in the recordings where the word is taught.

entries.definition: Being taken and held by enemies, the punishment the law foretells for disobedience (Deuteronomy 28:41): "such as are for the captivity, to the captivity" (Jeremiah 15:2). The classes teach that the Assyrian and Babylonian captivities (Matthew 1:17) were followed by a longer one after Rome destroyed Jerusalem (Luke 21:24), which they hold continues in the slavery and oppression of their people today, and that the nations who led Israel captive will go into captivity themselves (Revelation 13:10).

entries.definition: The penalties God set on Israel for breaking his commandments, listed chiefly in Deuteronomy 28:15-68 and Leviticus 26. The classes read them as their people's history: slavery, serving their enemies, sons and daughters given to another people (Deuteronomy 28:32), and being brought into Egypt again with ships (Deuteronomy 28:68). They teach that the curses are generational, "upon thy seed for ever" (Deuteronomy 28:46), and lift fully only at Christ's return, though keeping the commandments is required now.

entries.definition: The name given to Esau (Genesis 25:30; 36:1), meaning red, and to the nation descended from him. The teaching identifies Edom with the so-called white man and with Rome and the empires that came from it: the last ruling kingdom before Christ returns and the robbers of Israel of whom Obadiah speaks. The prophecies against Edom and Idumea (Isaiah 34:5, Ezekiel 35, Obadiah, Malachi 1:3-4) are read of that nation and its judgment.

entries.definition: Isaac's firstborn and Jacob's twin, who sold his birthright to Jacob for bread and pottage of lentiles (Genesis 25:33-34) and is the father of Edom (Genesis 36:8); Hebrews 12:16 calls him a profane person. The classes read 2 Esdras 6:9, "Esau is the end of the world, and Jacob is the beginning of it that followeth", to teach that Esau's seed holds the last ruling empire before the everlasting kingdom under Christ passes to Jacob, and trace Amalek and later nations from his line.

entries.definition: From "the four corners of the earth" (Isaiah 11:12; Revelation 7:1): the whole earth, the places to which Israel was scattered. The classes teach that the gospel must be taught to the scattered Israelites throughout the four corners of the earth before the end comes (Matthew 24:14), and that God gathers them from there (Isaiah 11:12).

entries.definition: The nations other than Israel. The classes identify them from the table of nations in Genesis 10 and the peoples named beside Israel, such as the Canaanites, Hittites, Moabites and Egyptians (Ezra 9:1). Where the New Testament speaks of Israelites "dispersed among the Gentiles" (John 7:35), of "Galilee of the Gentiles" (Matthew 4:15), or tells believers "ye were Gentiles" (1 Corinthians 12:2), the teaching reads it of Israelites scattered among the nations and living like them.

entries.definition: In the King James text, the nations that do not know or serve the God of Israel. The classes teach "learn not the way of the heathen" (Jeremiah 10:2) against holidays and customs taken from the nations, and read "why do the heathen rage" (Psalms 2:1) of the nations' hatred of Israel. Israel is to possess "the remnant of Edom, and of all the heathen" (Amos 9:12).

entries.definition: The descendants of Jacob, whom God named Israel (Genesis 32:28), through his twelve sons: the people God calls "my people" when he sends Moses to bring them out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10). The classes teach that the children of Israel are not the people occupying Jerusalem today but the so-called Blacks, Hispanics and Native Americans, scattered among the nations under the curses of the law, and that God has not ceased to count them a nation, for the sun and moon still stand (Jeremiah 31:35-36).

entries.definition: A title of God in the scriptures, "the most high God" (Genesis 14:18), and the classes' ordinary name for the God of Israel, heard in their greetings ("all praise to the Most High", "Most High and Christ bless"). The teaching draws from it that he does not change or break his covenant (Psalms 89:34), and that he rules in the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will (Daniel 4:17), which is why the earth is for now in Esau's hands.

entries.definition: A commandment or rule of God (Psalms 119:4). In the classes it chiefly names the method of study in Isaiah 28:10, "precept must be upon precept... line upon line; here a little, and there a little": a scripture is interpreted by the other scriptures that speak to it, not read like a novel. A verse brought in this way to support another is called a precept; "through thy precepts I get understanding" (Psalms 119:104).

entries.definition: The tribes descended from the twelve sons of Jacob (Genesis 49:28): the whole nation of Israel, divided after Solomon into two kingdoms, the "two families" of Jeremiah 33:24, and scattered. The classes teach that James writes "to the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad" (James 1:1), that Christ died to gather all twelve tribes and not the southern kingdom alone (John 11:52), and that all twelve will be joined again and saved (Ezekiel 37:16-22; Isaiah 45:17).
